beats.label: ETYMOLOGY

slides.text: Norbert Wiener, 1948. Cybernetics is born in the sky, solving a targeting problem.
slides.note:
→ "Let's go back to where the word comes from — and it's a longer road than you'd expect, so bear with the history for a few minutes."

→ "Start with Norbert Wiener. 1948. His book is called, simply, 'Cybernetics' — control and communication in the animal and the machine. Wiener's own path into this ran through anti-aircraft fire control in World War Two: predicting where a plane will be, not where it is, and closing the loop between sensor and gun in real time. Cybernetics is born in the sky, solving a targeting problem."
· The actual predictor/feedback-loop hardware Wiener worked from — sensor and gun closed into one loop.
· The book itself: control and communication in the animal and the machine.

slides.text: Marshall McLuhan: media as extensions of man.
slides.note: → "Marshall McLuhan picks up the same thread a generation later. 'Understanding Media,' 1964 — media as extensions of man. McLuhan's argument and Wiener's engineering are doing the same work from two directions: technology isn't a tool sitting outside you, it's a loop that runs through you."
· McLuhan, a generation after Wiener, arguing media are extensions of man.

slides.text: For the exogenously extended organizational complex functioning as an integrated homeostatic system unconsciously, we propose the term 'Cyborg.'
slides.attrib: Manfred Clynes & Nathan Kline, "Cyborgs and Space," 1960
slides.note:
→ "Coined in 1960 by Manfred Clynes and Nathan Kline, in a paper called 'Cyborgs and Space.'"

→ "They were solving a concrete NASA problem: how do you keep a human body alive in an environment that wants to destroy it."

→ "Their proposal wasn't to build a massive Earth-like chamber. It was to modify the human — biologically and technologically — and integrate them directly into the mechanical loops of the vehicle."

→ "Read it word by word. 'Exogenously extended' — the extension is outside the skin. 'Homeostatic system' — self-regulating. And 'unconsciously.'"

→ "That last word is load-bearing. The whole definition turns on the system running below attention. If you notice your prosthesis constantly, integration has failed."

slides.text: They were describing space travel. I'm describing your phone.
slides.note: → "They were describing space travel. I'm describing your smartphone."

slides.text: The word began as an engineering requirement.
slides.note:
→ "The word began as an engineering requirement."

⏱ Let it sit, then move.

beats.presenterNotes: ⏱ 8 min · Wiener → McLuhan → Clynes and Kline — the word started as a spec, not a metaphor and not science fiction

beats.label: CONTROL / STABILITY

cue.prompt: The capsule was built to fly itself. Then it didn't.

slides.alt: NACA test pilot and engineer reviewing flight data
slides.note: · This is the engineering culture Project Mercury was born into — slide rules and flight-test data, before a pilot ever touched the hardware.

slides.text: The capsule was built to fly itself. The pilots called it 'spam in a can.'
slides.note:
→ "Here's where the human-in-the-loop argument gets concrete — and it's the same story I planted back at the start of this talk."

→ "Project Mercury, America's first crewed spaceflight program, was designed, at first, around automation. The capsule was built to fly itself. The astronaut was mostly there to be monitored."

→ "The Mercury Seven were all military test pilots. Several had combat records. They hated this. Chuck Yeager — the first man to break the sound barrier, not one of the seven, but very much part of that culture — called the whole program 'spam in a can.' Being flown, not flying. That's the insult."

→ "They fought for it and won real concessions: a window — the original design didn't have one — and a manual control system as backup to the automatic one."
· A Mercury-program astronaut in the pressure suit they fought to be more than cargo inside.

slides.text: Carpenter flew the horizon by eye. Cooper flew reentry by wristwatch.
slides.note:
→ "That backup system was not decorative. Scott Carpenter, 1962 — his automatic attitude control failed mid-flight and bled fuel. He flew a good chunk of the mission on manual, eyeballing the window against the Earth's horizon."

→ "Gordon Cooper, the very last Mercury flight, 1963 — a cascading electrical failure killed the automatic system's power entirely. Cooper flew a fully manual reentry: hand controller, a grease-pencil mark on the window for his pitch angle, his own wristwatch for retrofire timing. It worked. By most accounts it was the most precise splashdown of the whole program."

slides.text: Neither side was wrong. Nobody won this argument by being right.
slides.attrib: resolved by the Cooper-Harper Handling Qualities Rating Scale, formalized 1969
slides.note:
→ "Neither side was wrong. The engineers were right that automation is safer on average. The pilots were right that a trained human is a hedge against exactly the failure automation can't predict. Nobody won this argument by being right."

→ "It got resolved by an actual piece of engineering that took the pilot's side seriously as a design input, not just a grudging backup switch: the Cooper-Harper Handling Qualities Rating Scale, built through the 1960s, formalized in 1969. A one-to-ten scale that converts a test pilot's subjective 'how did that feel' into a number an engineer can design against."

→ "It's still the industry standard today — aircraft, military helicopters, NASA spacecraft. A scale built to make a human's felt experience legible to a systems engineer, and vice versa. This is the connection I meant at the very start, when I said we design for the connections between elements in a system — human, agent, and stack."

slides.text: Apollo 11. The computer alarms. A 24-year-old with a handwritten list.
slides.note:
→ "Fast-forward six years. Apollo 11, July 1969. During the actual lunar landing, the guidance computer starts throwing alarms — 1202, 1201 — it's overloaded, dropping low-priority tasks."

→ "A 24-year-old engineer named Jack Garman has a handwritten list of alarm codes taped to his console. He tells Mission Control in seconds: survivable, keep going. That's a systems engineer's preparation, directly keeping the mission alive."

slides.text: Armstrong saw the boulder field and took the controls by hand.
slides.note: → "And then Neil Armstrong looks at where the automatic program is actually taking them — a boulder field — and takes manual control. Flies it by hand to a clear spot. Lands with less than a minute of fuel left, by some estimates."

slides.text: Both things were true in the same thirty seconds.
slides.note:
→ "Both things are true in the same thirty seconds. The engineered system — alarm triage, guidance computer, a checklist taped to a console — kept the mission alive. And the human pilot's judgment, trained into his body, faster than any checklist, made the call the machine couldn't make."

→ "That's not a contest. That's the actual shape of a cyborg system working."

⏱ Let this sit for a beat before moving to CYBERNETICS.

beats.presenterNotes:

beats.label: CYBERNETICS

cue.prompt: Where does your toolchain sit on this timeline?

slides.text: Feedback is the key. Feedback is the key to cybernetics, which is the key to the AI era.
slides.attrib: John Maeda, Design in Tech Report 2026, SXSW
slides.note:
→ "That's Maeda, at SXSW this year."

→ "Same underlying architecture across aircraft autopilot, car lane control, and coding-agent autoapprovals. The loop is the fundamental unit of an agentic system."

items: Closed loop — learning while you go
slides.note:
→ "Open loop means no feedback. Closed loop means learning while you're getting along."

→ "So if everything is feedback loops, interface design becomes conversation architecture. You're not designing screens — you're designing the terms of negotiation."

slides.text: Technology is anything we intentionally co-evolved.
slides.note:
→ "Technology is broad. Supercomputers and laptops, but also books, language and dialect."

→ "Cybernetics is the inflection point, because that's when technology starts talking back — and bidirectional influence becomes impossible to ignore."

→ "This is the DNA of McLuhan's argument. What's new is that the negotiation surface is now linguistic, which makes it obvious."

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 5 min · feedback → cybernetics → AI era

⏱ Student engagement, quick: "map your own tools onto this. Where does Figma sit? Where does a language model sit?" Take two answers from the feed, no more.

slides.title: CYBORG-LIVE — THE APP RUNNING THIS ROOM
beats: This SIGNAL/ASSEMBLE tool, built for Design Week RI, running again tonight.
Not "I asked an AI to build an app" — a named multi-agent stack, roles divided.
Fact-check before voice-edit, never after. Sequence changes what survives revision.
You're looking at the assemblage. It built the room you're standing in.
slides.note:
→ "The professor asked me to walk through what I'm actually building right now — so let's get concrete. Five short cases, same argument each time, different hands."

→ "You're looking at it. This SIGNAL and ASSEMBLE tool, built for Design Week RI, running again tonight — same zero-dependency engine, two completely separate decks, neither one touching the other."

That ordering matters: fact-check before voice-edit, never after, because sequence changes what survives revision. That discipline IS the stewardship the thesis names. An assemblage with roles, not one tool you operate."

slides.title: PONG3D — THE VIBE-CODE ORIGIN STORY
beats: Started as a test: run an agent in a loop, get a full game from one prompt.
With use, the process changed — the agent started choosing its own team.
One commit per slice, its own test suite embedded in the page.
The self-test isn't a feature. It's choosing what to verify and what to hand off.
slides.note:
→ "This one started as a test: could I run an agent in a loop and get a complete game out of one prompt? Then, with use, the process changed — the agent started determining its own team composition instead of me specifying it upfront."

→ "That shift is the steward's arc in miniature. One-prompt-one-shot to 'the system decides its own team.' The self-verifying build discipline — one commit per slice, its own test suite embedded in the page — that's what the process grew INTO. It wasn't there on day one."

→ "The self-test isn't a feature. It's me choosing what part of verification to keep and what part to hand off — the actual daily practice of being a steward instead of a user. And that discipline itself grew out of the vibe-code phase."

slides.alt: Ghost Field, THE DISTRICT track screenshot
slides.note: · Live screenshot from demos.marcelmcvay.com/ghost-field/, track 7 "THE DISTRICT."

slides.title: GHOST FIELD — THE ROADMAPPED DESIGN DOC
beats: A flight game, built under a named agent instance called RIG.
M1 flight core frozen and playable. M2.1 shipped. M2.2 is active right now.
"anime.js choreographs, Three.js renders" — an architecture decision, in writing.
The doc has me overriding RIG's scope creep — build the stage, not the play.
slides.note:
→ "Different process, same discipline. This is a flight game, built under a named agent instance called RIG, run the traditional way — real milestone docs written before anything got built. Flight core is frozen and playable. The city district shipped its first pass. The architecture milestone you're looking at right now — replacing placeholder boxes with a real city language — is what's actively in progress."

· Show the doc on screen here — the actual M2.2 architecture Q&A document. RIG proposes a lean under each design question; I confirm it or redirect it.

→ "Even the code libraries get roles in this build — the architecture doc literally says 'anime.js choreographs, Three.js renders.' That's not metaphor. That's the actual document."

· OPTIONAL, ~20 sec, cut first if short on time: there's a real moment in this doc where I catch RIG proposing scope creep — it wanted to build a whole vendor-and-collect gameplay loop into this milestone, and I redirected it back down to 'build the stage, not the play,' because that loop actually needs three other milestones of prerequisite work RIG hadn't accounted for.

slides.title: SPACE SANDBOX — ACCURATE ISN'T HONEST
beats: Two learning tools, one session: a space-policy timeline and a Voyager-scale tracker.
175 automated checks passed. Every object near Earth still read exactly 1.00 AU.
Correct, and it collapsed the ISS, the Moon, and a telescope into one dot.
The suite verifies the build. I verify the meaning. That's the integration.
slides.note:
→ "Two more, built in one session as learning tools for myself, not client work. One's a timeline of fifty-nine space-policy initiatives since a 2010 speech — four argument arcs, a glossary that links itself across every card. The other's a three.js map of everything we've sent into space, scoped to Voyager 1's actual distance — forty spacecraft, eight planets, ten moons."

→ "Here's the real story from building them, though: a hundred seventy-five automated browser checks ran clean, and the app was still wrong. Every object at Earth's distance read exactly one-point-oh AU. That's correct — heliocentrically, true. It's also useless, because it collapses the space station, the Moon, and a telescope a million miles out into the same dot. Accurate, and it lied."

→ "Catching that wasn't a bug fix. It was asking a different question: not 'is this correct,' but 'does this leave someone with a true picture.' That's the seat a human holds in this kind of system — not oversight of the machine, a different kind of verification running right next to it. The suite verifies the build. I verify the meaning. That's the integration."

→ "Both are running default Claude web-app styling right now — keen eyes in this room might already recognize it. Nobody specified this look. It just happened. So — what does it mean that it keeps happening? I want to open that up as a live activity: submit visual ideas, and we reskin one of these on the spot. The whole palette in each app is about a dozen lines at the top of one file, so this can genuinely happen live in under a minute."

· The audience app has a third COLLECTIVE tab for exactly this — a STYLE submission lane, plus a separate group-built ASCII text-adventure. First-draft prototype, test it live before trusting it cold.

slides.title: SOLAR WITNESS — THE EIGHT-ROLE AGENT TEAM
beats: Tracks human intervention across the solar system. Eight named agents, not one.
The expensive model went on whichever task fails silently — not the hardest-sounding one.
Designed as build, attack, fix — two passes. It took four.
Budget for the pass after the pass you think is last.
slides.note:
→ "One more, and this is the resource-stewardship case. Solar Witness tracks human intervention across the solar system — right now, a ninety-nine-entry catalog of lunar artifacts, with almost four hundred sourced citations. It was built by eight named agents, not one: an orchestrator, a coordinate-math specialist, a researcher, an adversarial verifier that never sees the researcher's reasoning and can't write to the file, an ongoing audit loop, an imagery specialist, and some cheap plumbing and recon roles."

→ "The expensive model didn't go on the hardest-sounding task. It went on whichever task fails silently. Bad coordinate math moves a lander a few kilometers and throws no error — that got the expensive model. Checking whether a URL returns 200 is either right or checkably wrong — that got the cheap one."

→ "Here's the real finding, though. The design was build, then attack, then fix — two passes. It took four. The verifier caught real defects, the builder fixed them. Then I caught one both of them missed: a stale source document still cited for the position of something that landed years after that document was written. The verifier had actually flagged the same class of problem in a different field — but the fix only covered that one instance, not the pattern. A fourth pass then found the same stale-source problem on fourteen more entries nobody had flagged."

→ "One error, four layers of checking, three of them turned out to be necessary. Budget for the pass after the pass you think is last."

· OPTIONAL second data point if the beat has room: a recon agent in this same build confidently reported that six data sources didn't support the kind of request the app needed. All six actually did. I only caught it by re-checking the claim myself. A subagent's confidence is not evidence.

slides.title: REGENT / THE SEAGLIDER
beats: Brief: an interface for a captain who can fly.
Then the test pilot showed up. Call sign: Bob Dylan.
"That's not where I expect it to be."
No agent. No model. No AI anywhere in this story.
slides.note:
→ "Last one, and it's different from everything else I just showed you. No agent. No model. No AI anywhere in this story."

→ "Regent builds a ground-effect craft that skims above the water — a captain that can fly, on paper. The brief called for a mariner at the controls. Then a test pilot joined — decades of hours, call sign a folksinger's name, we called him Bob Dylan."

→ "He liked every concept. Every concept was wrong — not messy, just mismatched with the logic his body had spent decades building. Pilots scan. They feel for what's off. They process feedback faster than conscious thought. His most common note: 'that's not where I expect it to be.'"

→ "I spent hours in a flight simulator learning how altimeters behave and where attitude indicators live. Every cockpit has a language, and I needed to be fluent enough to design in dialect. We ended with a recalibrated vocabulary, not a reinvented one."

→ "Here's why this one closes instead of opens, and it's the whole reason I put it last: every other case tonight was an AI build story. This one has none of that. It's a human pilot's embodied feedback loop, negotiated by a human designer, no model in sight."

→ "And that pilot, scanning his instruments faster than conscious thought — that's the exact NACA and NASA human-in-the-system note from the start of this talk. It's the same tension I told you about earlier tonight — ace pilots against systems engineers, Mercury astronauts fighting for manual control, Cooper-Harper turning felt experience into a design spec, Armstrong taking the controls by hand over a boulder field. Regent is that story again, just with no rocket involved."

→ "Assemblage integration means designing the negotiation, not the screen. And notice: nothing here was an AI system. The thesis was never about AI — AI is just the loudest, newest wire in the assemblage. The pilot and the instrument panel were already a cyborg circuit long before any of this was intelligent."
